question: Is anyone without sin?
summary: 1 Kings 8:46, 2 Chronicles 6:36, Proverbs 20:9, Ecclesiastes 7:20, Romans 3:23, and 1 John 1:8-10 all declare that no human is without sin. 1 John 3:6, 3:9, and 5:18 declare that anyone born of God does not sin and cannot sin. The Johannine epistles internally affirm both that all sin and that the regenerate do not sin.

reconcile.connective: Commentators harmonize by sense: "cannot sin" denies habitual, dominating sin (the new nature), not the occasional acts every believer must still confess.

discrepancy.connective: The sharpest objection is pressed by Raymond E. Brown, who argues that 1 John affirms both that all sin and that the begotten cannot sin, with no author contradicting himself so sharply in so short a span.

skeptic.name: Raymond E. Brown
skeptic.attribution: Raymond E. Brown (d. 1998), The Epistles of John, Anchor Bible 30 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1982)

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871), on 1 John 3:9
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treat this exact internal tension at 1 John 3:9, stating it 'does not contradict' 1 John 1:8-9 and reconciling the begotten nature's incompatibility with sin against the believer's actual lapses. Used as the row-surfaced harmonizing commentator keyed to the passage, since Haley's coverage of this specific 1 John crux could not be confirmed.

link.title: Defending Inerrancy: Is there a Bible contradiction in 1 John 3:9?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment citing both 1 John 3:9 and 1 John 1:8; harmonizes via the present-continuous reading ('does not continually practice sin').

excerpts.excerpt_text: This does not contradict Jo1 1:8-9; the regenerate show the utter incompatibility of sin with regeneration, by cleansing away every sin into which they may be betrayed by the old nature, at once in the blood of Christ.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB names both poles by reference (1:8-9 'all sin' vs 3:9 'cannot sin') and explicitly denies they contradict, reading the begotten nature as incompatible with sin while the believer still falls and is cleansed.
excerpts.source_note_text:
Whosoever is born of God--literally, "Everyone that is begotten of God."
doth not commit sin--His higher nature, as one born or begotten of God, doth not sin. To be begotten of God and to sin, are states mutually excluding one another. In so far as one sins, he makes it doubtful whether he be born of God.
his seed--the living word of God, made by the Holy Spirit the seed in us of a new life and the continual mean of sanctification.
remaineth--abideth in him (compare Note, see on Jo1 3:6; Joh 5:38). This does not contradict Jo1 1:8-9; the regenerate show the utter incompatibility of sin with regeneration, by cleansing away every sin into which they may be betrayed by the old nature, at once in the blood of Christ.
cannot sin, because he is born of God--"because it is of God that he is born" (so the Greek order, as compared with the order of the same words in the beginning of the verse); not "because he was born of God" (the Greek is perfect tense, which is present in meaning, not aorist); it is not said, Because a man was once for all born of God he never afterwards can sin; but, Because he is born of God, the seed abiding now in Him, he cannot sin; so long as it energetically abides, sin can have no place. Compare Gen 39:9, Joseph, "How CAN I do this great wickedness and sin against God?" The principle within me is at utter variance with it. The regenerate life is incompatible with sin, and gives the believer a hatred for sin in every shape, and an unceasing desire to resist it. "The child of God in this conflict receives indeed wounds daily, but never throws away his arms or makes peace with his deadly foe" [LUTHER]. The exceptional sins into which the regenerate are surprised, are owing to the new life principle being for a time suffered to lie dormant, and to the sword of the Spirit not being drawn instantly. Sin is ever active, but no longer reigns. The normal direction of the believer's energies is against sin; the law of God after the inward man is the ruling principle of his true self though the old nature, not yet fully deadened, rebels and sins. Contrast Jo1 5:18 with Joh 8:34; compare Psa 18:22-23; Psa 32:2-3; Psa 119:113, Psa 119:176. The magnetic needle, the nature of which is always to point to the pole, is easily turned aside, but always reseeks the pole.
